unit.title: Bubbles and crises
unit.description: From tulips to FTX: what happened in each crisis and what rules it left us
unit.section: A history of crises and bubbles

u34l1.title: Tulips and the South Sea Company

texts: A bulb worth a house
Pieter, merchant
The Dutch Republic (today's Netherlands), winter 1636-1637.
This rare tulip bulb is already worth as much as a house. And next week, even more!
Don't plant it: sell it on to someone else for more. Everyone's doing it.
What do you do?
I buy: there'll always be someone who'll pay more
That's the **greater fool theory**: it works until there's nobody left.
I'm not paying the price of a house for a bulb just because it's rising
Good. The price had come completely loose from what it was worth.
I buy just one, just in case
Better than ten. But you're still betting on finding someone who'll pay more.
February 1637: the buyers vanish and prices collapse.
Historians argue about how many people were ruined, but it's the classic bubble.
Newton and the South Sea
Isaac Newton
London, 1720. South Sea Company shares go from about 128 pounds in January to over 1,000 in the summer.
I sold at a profit… and it's still going up. My friends are getting rich.
They say this time it's different: trade with South America has no limit.
What do you advise him?
Get back in: don't miss out
That's what he did. By the end of the year, the shares were back at January levels.
Stay out: the price has nothing to do with the business any more
Wise. He didn't: he bought back in near the top.
Get in with a loan, to make money faster
Debt in the middle of a frenzy: the recipe for ruin.
Newton bought back in at a high price and lost about 20,000 pounds. He's credited with this line:
I can calculate the motion of heavenly bodies, but not the madness of people.

steps.title: The eternal pattern
steps.body:
A real or promised novelty → rising prices → people buying just because it's rising → easy credit → «this time it's different» → nobody else buys → a rapid fall.

When you buy something only because you think someone else will pay you more for it, you're already inside a bubble.
steps.key: Bubbles change their costume, but they follow the same script.
steps.tip: Try it: before your next purchase, tell your tutor Lumi why you are making it.

texts: Live through the 1929 crash
January 1929: the US stock market is riding the euphoria of the Roaring Twenties. You invest **€10,000** in the S&P 500, **with no debt**, and follow it week by week until 1955 with real data.
From the September 1929 peak, how far did the market fall at its worst?
More than 80 %
After Black Thursday (24 October) and Black Tuesday (the 29th), the S&P 500 fell **83 %** by July 1932, and the Dow Jones 89 %.
Go all the way to 1955, whether you sell or not.

In June 1932 your €10,000 was worth **about €1,830**. With no debt you could wait: the Dow Jones didn't get back to its 1929 peak until **1954**, about 25 years without dividends (about 15 with dividends and deflation).
You've sold. See what happens next…
Your €10,000 is worth less than €3,000. Can you hold on?
Down 20 %. Anyone who bought on credit no longer has a choice.
Everything's going up. What if it were with borrowed money?
Hit start. You can sell whenever you like
Buying with 10 %
In the '20s, lots of people bought shares **on credit**: they put in around **10 %** and the broker lent them the rest. You put in €1,000.
With €1,000 of your own and €9,000 borrowed, the shares fall 10 %. What are you left with?
About €900
Nothing
About €500
The shares are worth €9,000, exactly what you owe. At ×10, **a −10 % move in the price is −100 %** of your money.
At ×10, find the fall that wipes out all your money.

With loans, a small drop wiped out everything and **brokers forced people to sell**; that forced selling pushed prices down even further. **Leverage turns a fall into ruin.** Try it: in your Portfolio, look at your cash: investing only with your own money lets you wait.
Everything's gone, and the price has only dropped a little.
With a small loan, a fall hurts, but it doesn't ruin you.
Move the price down
Live through the dot-com bubble
December 1998: any company with «.com» shoots up, whether it makes money or not. You invest **€10,000** in the Nasdaq 100 and follow it week by week with real data.
In March 2000, your €10,000 is worth over €25,000. How much will be left by autumn 2002?
About €20,000
About €10,000
Less than €5,000
**About €4,440**: from its peak, the Nasdaq 100 fell more than 80 %.
Go all the way to the end, whether you sell or not.
The internet really did change the world: the idea was good. **The problem was the price**, and the Nasdaq took about 15 years, until 2015, to get back to its peak.
You've sold. See what happens next…
Less than €6,000 of your 10,000. Can you hold on?
More than doubled. Do you take some profit, or is «this time different»?
Hit start. You can sell whenever you like
March 2000
Javi
I've got 100 % of my savings in tech funds. +300 % in three years!
My brother-in-law says I should sell «even just a bit». The internet is the future, right?
What do you tell him?
No selling: the internet is the future
It was. And even so, the Nasdaq fell nearly 78 %.
Go back to a diversified mix: less tech and some bonds
You don't need to guess the top: you just need not to depend on one expensive sector.
Take out a loan and buy more
Debt, concentration and sky-high prices: the most dangerous combination.
Pets.com goes public in February 2000 and shuts down that November. Amazon falls more than 90 %… and survives.
A great company can be a bad investment if you pay too much for it.
Try it: look at your Portfolio. If a single sector is more than half, spread it out.
A mortgage for everyone
Mortgage broker
United States, 2006. Millions of **subprime** mortgages are handed out: to people with little ability to repay.
No need to check their income. Mortgage approved, today.
Then we bundle it with thousands of others and sell it all over the world. The agencies rate it «very safe».
What could go wrong?
Nothing: house prices always go up
When house prices fell, defaults soared.
If house prices fall, lots of people won't pay and those securities will collapse
Exactly. And those securities were held by heavily indebted banks all over the world.
It only affects whoever signs
If only. That **securitisation** spread the risk all over the world.
15 September 2008: Lehman Brothers goes bust. Panic spreads and credit freezes.
Even the experts got it wrong. If you don't understand a product, you don't know its risk.
Ride out the 2008 crisis
October 2007: **€10,000** in the S&P 500, with real data. You have a cushion, you owe nothing and you won't need the money for years.
Go all the way to the end without selling.

In March 2009 your €10,000 was worth **about €4,390** (−56 %), and without selling it was back to €10,000 in March 2013, without dividends. **With a cushion and no debt, a fall doesn't force you to sell.** Try it: set an alert 20 % below the price of the S&P 500 ETF and decide today what you will do.
You've sold. When it ends, try again and see if you can hold on.
Lehman has gone bust and people are talking about another Great Depression.
Down 20 %. Your cushion covers your expenses: you don't need to sell.
Hit start and hold on
Live through Japan's bubble
January 1985: Japan is the economy everyone's talking about and its stock market keeps climbing. You invest **€10,000** in the Nikkei 225 and follow it month by month, with real data, until 2025.
By the end of 1989, your €10,000 is about €32,000. How long will it take the Nikkei to get back to that peak?
About 5 years
About 15 years
More than 30 years
It closed at **38,915 points** on 29 December 1989 and didn't top that until **February 2024: 34 years later**.
Go all the way to the end, whether you sell or not.

In March 2009, the Nikkei was **82 %** below its peak. **A rich, advanced country can go decades without recovering**: «the stock market always recovers» only holds with time, diversification and no debt.
You've sold. See what happens next…
Years later, it's worth less than you put in.
More than double. Could anything stop this?
Hit start. You can sell whenever you like
Investing in what you know
Kenji
Tokyo, 1990. Japan is the biggest stock market in the world.
I've got all my savings in the Nikkei. I invest in what I know: Japan.
My cousin has hers spread all over the world. What a hassle!
Who do you think will be better off in 20 years?
Kenji: he invests in what he knows
Twenty years later, the Nikkei was still way below its peak.
His cousin: she doesn't depend on a single country
Exactly: the rest of the world had far better decades than Japan.
Both the same: the stock market is the stock market
One country and the world can perform very differently for decades.
A global index doesn't depend on any one country doing well.
Try it: in Market, compare the Nikkei 225 chart with that of a global ETF.

u34l6.title: Spain: the housing bubble and the risk premium

texts: Live through Spain's crisis
December 2006: the property boom is in full swing and credit is easy. You invest **€10,000** in the IBEX 35 and follow it month by month, with real data, until 2025.
First comes the 2008 crisis and then, in Spain, another one right behind it. At the worst point, what's your investment worth?
A bit less: about €8,500
Less than half
More than at the start
In May 2012 it was worth **about €4,305**: −57 %, not counting dividends.
Go all the way to the end, whether you sell or not.

Not counting dividends, the IBEX 35 didn't get back to its late-2006 level until **2025**. Dividends helped a lot, but **people who only held Spanish shares suffered more** than those diversified around the world.
You've sold. See what happens next…
Less than half. Hold on or sell?
The savings banks (cajas) lent far too much to property.
Hit start. You can sell whenever you like
July 2012
Your dad
Mario Draghi (ECB)
I've got everything in Spanish shares and I've lost half. They're saying Spain will leave the euro.
The risk premium goes over 600 points: the Spanish bond pays more than 7 %.
What do you tell him?
Sell everything and never invest again
Selling at peak fear turns the fall into a real loss.
Don't panic sell, and from now on diversify around the world
Good: the mistake wasn't investing, it was having everything in one country.
Move everything into Spanish bonds at 7 %
Swapping one bet on Spain for another bet on Spain doesn't fix anything.
26 July 2012, London.
The ECB is ready to do whatever it takes to preserve the euro. And believe me, it will be enough.
Risk premium: how much more Spain pays than Germany. 100 points = 1 %.
Try it: in Market, compare the IBEX 35 with an MSCI World ETF.
Live through the COVID crash
January 2020: you invest **€10,000** in the S&P 500 and follow it day by day with real data. Then comes a pandemic nobody saw coming.
From the 19 February peak to the bottom, how long did the 34 % fall take?
A week
Just over a month
A year
**33 days**: it hit bottom on 23 March 2020. The fastest fall in its history.
Go all the way to the end, whether you sell or not.
And the fastest recovery: by 18 August 2020 the S&P 500 was already at record highs, **about 5 months later**. Anyone who sold «until things become clearer» missed a big chunk of the rebound.
You've sold. See what happens next…
Hospitals full and the economy shut down. Sell or hold on?
Half the world goes into lockdown. Central banks and governments prepare huge stimulus.
Hit start. You can sell whenever you like
16 March 2020
Dani
My portfolio has fallen 25 % in three weeks. The news is terrifying.
I won't need it for 15 years, but I'm selling everything and I'll get back in when the pandemic's over.
What do you tell him?
Good idea: get back in when things are clearer
By the time it «was over», the market was already at record highs: you sell low and buy back high.
If you won't need it for years, stick to your plan and your contributions
The boring stuff worked: within 5 months the S&P 500 was at record highs.
Take out a loan and buy as much as you can
Nobody knew the bottom was close. With debt, another fall forces you to sell.
According to J.P. Morgan, 7 of the S&P 500's 10 best days between 2005 and 2024 came within two weeks of one of the 10 worst.
Nobody can predict the bottom. Panic selling was the big mistake of 2020.
Try it: tell your tutor Lumi what you will do if your Portfolio falls 25 %.
Live through the crypto winter
December 2020: you invest **€10,000** in bitcoin. Your investment tracks its dollar price, week by week, until 2025.
November 2021: your €10,000 is nearly €20,000. What will it be worth a year later?
More than €30,000
About the same
About €5,000
In November 2022 it was worth **about €4,970**: bitcoin fell 75 % from its peak on these weekly closes.
Go all the way to the end, whether you sell or not.

Bitcoin dropped from nearly $69,000 to about $15,500 (−77 %) and many cryptos fell more than 90 %. This series recovered later, but crypto isn't regulated like a deposit: **you can lose everything you've invested**.
You've sold. See what happens next…
Terra collapses in May and FTX goes bust in November 2022.
Nearly double or more. And how much could you lose?
Hit start. You can sell whenever you like
A «stable» 20 %
Irene
Exchange
My platform pays almost 20 % a year, stable, with a coin pegged to the dollar.
What do you tell her?
Great: stable and at 20 %
A «stable» 20 % is a sign of risk, not of safety.
A stable 20 % is a red flag: where does it come from?
Well spotted! That was Terra, with its algorithmic stablecoin UST.
Move it to a big exchange, it's like a bank
It isn't: there's no deposit guarantee scheme for your crypto.
May 2022: UST loses its peg to the dollar. Within days, Terra and LUNA lose almost all their value: around 40,000 million dollars.
Withdrawals temporarily paused. Your funds are safe.
Celsius and other platforms freeze withdrawals and go bust. In November FTX collapses after using its customers' money; its founder is sentenced to 25 years.
«Not your keys, not your coins.»
Try it: look at your Portfolio. Crypto should be a small part you could afford to lose.

u34l9.title: What all crises have in common

texts: Does it help you or sink you?
Tulips, 1929, 2000, 2008, crypto… The next crisis arrives. What **helps** you get through it and what **sinks** you?
Helps you
Sinks you
A cushion of 6 months' expenses
You won't have to sell at the worst moment to pay the bills.
Having invested with borrowed money
In 1929, credit forced people to sell at the worst moment.
A portfolio spread around the world
Japan in 1989 and Spain in 2012: a single country can sink for years.
Selling in the middle of a panic
In 2009 and 2020, people who sold at the worst point missed the rebound.
A written investment plan
You write it while calm so you can stick to it in a panic.
Having everything in the trend of the moment
Dot-coms in 2000, crypto in 2021: today's trend can be tomorrow's bubble.
Not paying any price
In 2000 the idea was good; the price wasn't.
Sort the seven things.
The script almost always repeats: a **novelty**, **easy credit**, **euphoria** («this time it's different»), a burst and **panic**. What protects you is prepared **before** the crisis.
Hint: think about who each crisis saved or sank.
Sort each one
Diversifying through crises
Real data since 2008, with dividends and coupons: US shares, bonds and gold. You start with everything in shares.
US shares (S&P 500)
US bonds
Gold
With everything in shares since 2008, how far did the portfolio fall at its worst?
Almost half
It never fell
**−46 %** in the 2008 crisis. Even so, anyone who held on multiplied their money almost 7 times (+593 %).
Split it between the three until the worst fall is no more than 25 %.
With **50 % shares, 30 % bonds and 20 % gold**, the worst fall was **22 %** and the portfolio gained 383 %. Less of a scare and less gain: **a fall you can stomach is a fall you don't sell in**.
Less of a scare. See how much gain you give up in return.
All in shares: look at the 2008 slump.
Move the weights and watch the worst fall

steps.title: The five rules
steps.body:
1. Don't invest with borrowed money.
2. Diversify across companies, sectors and countries.
3. Keep an emergency fund so you never have to sell.
4. Don't pay any price.
5. Don't panic sell: if your plan is a 20-year one, a fall lasting months doesn't change it.

Crises don't give warning, but you can prepare for them.
steps.key: Those who were diversified, debt-free and patient recovered from every crisis.
steps.tip: Try it: check your Portfolio against the five rules and fix any you are breaking.

s12boss.title: Final challenge: A history of crises and bubbles

u34l1-1.prompt: Put the typical stages of a bubble in order.
options: Prices rise and attract more buyers
The first ones sell and buyers stop coming in
Euphoria: people buy just because it's rising, often on credit
u34l1-1.explanation: It's the pattern described by economists like Kindleberger and Minsky: it repeats century after century.

u34l1-2.prompt: Where and when did tulip mania happen?
options: In the Dutch Republic (the Netherlands), around 1637
u34l1-2.explanation: London 1720 is the South Sea Company.

u34l1-6.prompt: Match each bubble with the promise that fuelled it.
u34l1-6.explanation: The product changes; the psychology is the same.
right: The internet
Digital currencies and NFTs
Trade with South America
Bulbs of rare tulips

u34l1-7.prompt: The phrase that pops up in almost every bubble is «this time it's ____».
u34l1-7.explanation: Every generation believes its novelty breaks the rules.

u34l1-9.prompt: Sign of a bubble or of a healthy market?
options: People taking out loans to get in
«This time it's different, the old rules don't apply»
A reasonable valuation relative to what the company earns
Everyone's talking about it, even people who've never invested
The price rises in line with profits
u34l1-9.explanation: Euphoria, credit and ignoring valuations are the classic alarm bells.
right: Bubble sign
Healthy sign

u34l1-10.prompt: What do you say to Lumi?
options: If my hairdresser is making money, it must be easy
Then I'm getting in now, before it's too late!
When everyone's talking about something, it's usually a sign of euphoria, not opportunity
u34l1-10.explanation: Widespread euphoria is an alarm bell, not an invitation.
feedback: Something having gone up doesn't make it easy or safe.
When even people who never invest are in, who's left to buy?
Well spotted! It's been one of the classic signs of a bubble since 1637.
lines: My neighbour bought a car with what he made on a new coin 🤑
And my hairdresser's got in too!

u34l2-1.prompt: This is how the S&P 500 moved from January 1928 to the summer of 1929. What trend do you see? (S&P 500 · weekly closes · up to the week of 30/09/1929)
u34l2-1.explanation: Almost two years of gains that made people think it would never end.

u34l2-2.prompt: It's 29 September 1929. The S&P 500 has just had a huge rise and lots of people have bought on credit. What did it do over the next three years?
u34l2-2.explanation: What happened next depended on something the chart doesn't show: how many people had bought with borrowed money.

u34l2-3.prompt: Tap the highest point before the crash. (S&P 500 · weekly closes · up to the week of 30/09/1929)
u34l2-3.explanation: From that peak began one of the biggest falls in stock market history.

options: Black Thursday and Black Tuesday, in October 1929
The Dow gets back to its peak in 1954
Euphoria of the '20s and buying on credit
u34l2-8.explanation: The rise took years; the fall, just a few; the recovery, decades without dividends.

u34l2-10.prompt: It's 1930. The stock market has fallen 40 %. Ana owes nothing and won't need the money for years. Bruno bought on credit and his broker is asking for more collateral. Who has more options?
options: Ana: with no debt, nobody can force her to sell
Both the same: it's the same stock market
Bruno, because if he puts in more money he can recover more
u34l2-10.explanation: Not investing with borrowed money is the first rule history teaches us.
feedback: Exactly. Time is only on your side if you can wait.
Same market, opposite situations: debt decides who can hold on.
Bruno has to put in money he may not have or sell at the worst moment. And there was still more to fall.

u34l3-1.prompt: This is how the Nasdaq 100 moved between late 1997 and March 2000. What trend do you see? (Nasdaq 100 · weekly closes · up to the week of 06/03/2000)
u34l3-1.explanation: It more than quadrupled in just over two years: enthusiasm for the internet seemed to have no ceiling.

u34l3-2.prompt: It's 6 March 2000. The Nasdaq 100 has more than quadrupled in two years thanks to the internet. What did it do over the next two and a half years?
u34l3-2.explanation: The internet really did change the world; the question was whether those prices already priced in all that future and more.
u34l3-2.horizon: the next two and a half years

u34l3-7.prompt: What became of these dot-com era companies?
u34l3-7.explanation: Pets.com shut down in 2000 and Webvan went bust in 2001. Picking the survivors in advance was almost impossible: another reason to diversify.
right: Survived
Disappeared

u34l3-9.prompt: What signs of a bubble were there in 1999-2000? Select all that apply.
options: Lots of new people buying just because it was rising
IPOs that doubled in price on the first day
Companies with no profits valued in the billions
u34l3-9.explanation: Valuations were forgotten: «the old rules don't apply any more».

u34l3-10.prompt: What do you say to Lumi?
options: Yes, just like the internet in 2000
The technology can be real and the price can still be too high
u34l3-10.explanation: Being right about a technology doesn't guarantee being right about the investment.
feedback: In 2000 the internet did change everything… and the Nasdaq fell 78 %.
You don't need to decide whether it's a fad: just don't pay any price and diversify.
That's it! What matters isn't just the idea, but how much you pay for it.
lines: Artificial intelligence is going to change everything 🤖
So any AI company is a good buy, right?

u34l4-1.prompt: Put the chain of events of the 2008 crisis in order.
options: House prices fall and defaults rise
Heavily indebted banks pile up losses
They're bundled into highly rated securities and sold around the world
Lehman Brothers goes bust and panic breaks out
Mortgages are given to people who could hardly afford them
u34l4-1.explanation: A chain in which each link amplified the one before.

u34l4-2.prompt: It's 8 September 2008, one week before Lehman Brothers collapsed. The S&P 500 has already fallen quite a lot from its peak. What did it do over the following year?
u34l4-2.explanation: At that point nobody knew whether the worst was over: the chart only shows the past.

u34l4-3.prompt: It's 2 March 2009. The S&P 500 has fallen more than 50 % and the headlines are talking about a new Great Depression. What did it do over the following months?
u34l4-3.explanation: At that point fear was everywhere and nobody knew whether the fall was over.

u34l4-5.prompt: Match each term with its meaning.
u34l4-5.explanation: The four pieces of the 2008 puzzle.
right: Bundling loans into securities that are sold on
Investment bank that went bust on 15 September 2008
Company that grades the risk of a security
Mortgage with a high risk of default

u34l4-10.prompt: What made the 2008 crisis much worse? Select all that apply.
options: Complex products that hardly anyone understood
u34l4-10.explanation: Leverage and complexity turned a mortgage problem into a global crisis.

u34l5-1.prompt: This is how Japan's Nikkei 225 moved between 1985 and late 1989. What trend do you see? (Nikkei 225 · monthly closes · up to December 1989)
u34l5-1.explanation: It more than tripled in five years: it seemed Japan could never stop growing.

u34l5-2.prompt: Late 1989: the Nikkei 225 has tripled in five years and Japan is the largest stock market in the world. What did it do over the next six years?
u34l5-2.explanation: A strong economy doesn't guarantee a rising stock market: it also depends on how much you pay for it.

u34l5-9.prompt: What do you say to Lumi?
options: Better to put everything in Japan, it's recovered now
Exactly, the US will never let you down
Japan also «always recovered»: better not to depend on a single country
u34l5-9.explanation: The US story is the story of the market that has done best. There's no guarantee it'll repeat.
feedback: Switching country is still concentrating.
In 1989 people said the same about Japan, and its stock market took 34 years to get back.
Nice! A global index already includes the US and covers you if it has its own lost decade.
lines: So I'll put everything in it and I don't need to diversify, right?

u34l5-10.prompt: What did the Japanese bubble have? Select all that apply.
options: Shares and land prices soaring at the same time
u34l5-10.explanation: It was the largest stock market in the world, not a small one.

u34l5-11.prompt: It is 1990. The Nikkei has already started to fall from its 1989 peak and a friend tells you: «Japan is the biggest stock market in the world and it always recovers: put all your savings here». What do you do?
options: I put everything in the Nikkei: Japan always recovers
I take out a loan to buy more now that it has fallen
I invest spread across the whole world, with Japan as just one part
u34l5-11.explanation: Spreading across countries protects you from picking the wrong one. The tempting one, «it always recovers», fails because a country can take decades: Japan took 34 years.
feedback: The Nikkei did not beat its 1989 peak until February 2024: a 34-year wait.
With debt you cannot wait for decades: you would be forced to sell long before.
Good: if one country has its lost decade, the rest of the portfolio keeps going.

u34l6-1.prompt: This is how the IBEX 35 moved from January 2010 to July 2012. What trend do you see? (IBEX 35 · weekly closes · up to the week of 23/07/2012)
u34l6-1.explanation: Two and a half years of debt crisis: from around 12,000 points to below 6,300.

u34l6-2.prompt: It's the last week of July 2012. Spain's risk premium is above 600 points and there's talk of a full bailout of Spain. What did the IBEX 35 do over the next year and a half?
u34l6-2.explanation: In the middle of a panic, prices already reflect an enormous amount of fear: what happens next depends on what nobody knows yet.
u34l6-2.horizon: the next year and a half

options: The difference between the interest on the Spanish and German 10-year bonds
u34l6-4.explanation: It measures how much more investors demand to lend to Spain than to Germany.

u34l6-6.prompt: Match each player with their role in the 2010-2012 crisis.
u34l6-6.explanation: Banks, public debt and the euro: three crises linked together.
right: Up to €100,000 million to clean up the banks
Gap with the German 10-year bond
Heavily exposed to property lending
«Whatever it takes» to save the euro

u34l6-9.prompt: Draghi said he would do «whatever it ____» to save the euro.
u34l6-9.explanation: The three most famous words of the euro crisis, on 26 July 2012.

u34l6-10.prompt: What lessons does the Spanish crisis leave? Select all that apply.
options: Concentrating on your own country protects you
Selling at peak fear usually turns out to be expensive
Easy credit and property can form a bubble
Your own country can have a very harsh crisis too
u34l6-10.explanation: Concentrating at home doesn't protect you: it concentrates your risk.

u34l7-1.prompt: Tap the S&P 500's peak before the COVID fall. (S&P 500 · daily closes · to 25/03/2020)
u34l7-1.explanation: 19 February 2020: almost nobody expected what would happen over the following weeks.

u34l7-2.prompt: Now tap the lowest point of the fall. (S&P 500 · daily closes · to 25/03/2020)
u34l7-2.explanation: Late March 2020: −34 % in just over a month from the peak.

u34l7-3.prompt: It's 25 March 2020. The S&P 500 has just fallen 34 % in a month, hospitals are filling up and the economy is shut down. What did it do over the following months?
u34l7-3.explanation: The day's news and stock prices don't always move together: the market looks months ahead.

u34l7-8.prompt: What do you say to Lumi?
options: It happened to loads of people: next time, decide in advance with a written plan
The best thing is never to invest again
Bad luck, next time you'll call the bottom
u34l7-8.explanation: You write the plan when you're calm so you can stick to it when you're panicking.
feedback: That's it! Your Investment Policy Statement exists for exactly that moment.
That way the mistake of March 2020 would also cost you every year that followed.
Calling the bottom is almost impossible: nobody announced it in advance.
lines: I was planning to get back in when it fell further… and it never did.
